paper.title: Frequency and laminar profile of feature-specific visual activity revealed by interleaved EEG–fMRI

nodes.text: Clausner et al. 2025, eLife 14:RP108408
nodes.description: Research article reporting interleaved simultaneous EEG-fMRI study of laminar feature-specific visual activity in human V1.
nodes.anchor: Clausner et al. eLife 2025;14:RP108408. DOI: https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.108408

nodes.text: Interleaved simultaneous EEG-fMRI with visual oddball task in 52 healthy participants
nodes.description: Main experiment: 240 trials (4 blocks × 60) of left/right oriented gratings (±45°) with 16.7% oddball wavy targets; 3T Siemens Prismafit, 64-channel EEG, 3D gradient-EPI with CAIPI (TR=3.3s, 3s gap for EEG), laminar fMRI of V1.
nodes.anchor: The main experiment consisted of four blocks of 60 trials each, ten of which were oddball trials that were excluded from the later analysis.

nodes.text: Population receptive field mapping for V1/V2/V3 identification
nodes.description: Three blocks of 128 trials each using moving chequered bars (2.25° wide, 18° long) in 4 directions; same fMRI sequence without EEG gaps; analyzed with analyzePRF toolbox.
nodes.anchor: Three blocks of population receptive field (pRF) mapping (128 trials each) have been performed after the main experiment using the same fMRI sequence as in the main experiment (without gaps).

nodes.text: Interleaved 3D gradient-EPI with CAIPI acceleration (TR=3.3s, TE=34ms, 0.9mm iso) and 3s gap every 3 volumes for artifact-free EEG
nodes.description: Partial brain coronal slab (208.8×208.8×39.6mm) covering occipital/parietal lobes; flip angle 20°; 6 dummy volumes per block (last 3 recorded); arbitrary delay between volume triplets set to 3s for EEG acquisition; BOLD HRF sampled after gap.

nodes.text: Visual oddball task with oriented gratings (±45°) and wavy pattern oddballs (16.7%), central fixation with blink control
nodes.description: Tukey-filtered gratings 8° diameter, 3.125 cycles/°, 70% contrast, 0.8° central cutout for fixation; oddballs: wavy pattern amplitude 0.3571°, frequency 0.6526 cycles/°, 4 phase offsets; fixation indicator (Greek cross) red/green for blink avoidance; 1.2s pre-stimulus red fixation, 1.6s stimulus, 0.6s post-stimulus; response via right index finger.
nodes.anchor: Participants performed a demanding visual attention task, using central stimulus presentation. The stimuli could either be left (counter-clockwise) or right (clockwise) oriented gratings (±45° relative to the vertical axis of the screen). A subtle wavy pat

nodes.text: LCMV beamforming of EEG to V1 grey matter voxels with FEM head model and curvature-derived dipole orientations
nodes.description: Separate processing for alpha (2-32 Hz) and gamma (20-120 Hz, 50Hz DFT filter); photogrammetry-based electrode localization (janus3D); FEM from T1 (FieldTrip-SimBio); leadfield from electrode positions and FEM; dipoles at V1 voxel locations with orientations from surface normals (Workbench); separate left/right hemisphere filters; virtual channels at dipole locations.
nodes.anchor: A finite element model (FEM) was computed from the high resolution anatomical T1 based on the FieldTrip-SimBio pipeline. The leadfield was computed from the EEG electrode positions and the FEM model. Sources were modelled as equivalent current dipoles at l

nodes.text: Time-frequency analysis of virtual channels: Hanning taper (400ms, 20ms steps, 0.5Hz resolution, ±2Hz smoothing) for alpha; multitaper DPSS (7 tapers, 2.5Hz resolution, ±10Hz smoothing) for gamma
nodes.description: Baseline: -0.3 to -0.1s for gamma, single bin at -0.3s for alpha (gradient artifacts prevented earlier baseline); log10 ratio to baseline; time window 0.1-1.6s post-stimulus; per hemisphere, select virtual channel with strongest alpha decrease (8-12Hz) and gamma increase (50-70Hz) relative to baseline.
nodes.anchor: While for low frequencies, a Hanning taper was applied using a data time window length of 400 ms (time steps: 20 ms), zero-padded to achieve a frequency resolution of 0.5 Hz and smoothed with a kernel width of ±2 Hz; for high frequencies the data was proce

nodes.text: Trial-by-trial EEG-fMRI GLM: z-transformed EEG TF power convolved with SPM12 HRF as parametric modulators; separate model per TF bin; fixed task/nuisance regressors
nodes.description: Nuisance: non-task trials, blinks, button presses, reaction times (parametric), white matter/residual signals, motion parameters + derivatives, 5 sine/cosine high-pass cycles; Task: left, right, both orientations; EEG regressors: 4 virtual channels × frequency bins (0.5Hz alpha, 2.5Hz gamma) × time bins (0.4s, 0.1s slide); onset at bin center shifted 1-3 TRs; voxel time courses z-transformed per block; GLM per voxel per block; β coefficients weighted by layer fractions; averaged across hemispheres, blocks, percentiles, time bins (0.1-0.8s).
nodes.anchor: One regressor was built for each frequency and time bin separately. This was done by convolving z-transformed trial-by-trial power changes of the EEG data with the haemodynamic response function that comes with SPM12, such that each regressor served as par

nodes.text: Curvature-corrected laminar segmentation: 5 shell-like meshes (CSF, superficial, middle, deep, white matter) between pial/white matter boundaries; voxel weights = volume fraction per layer
nodes.description: FreeSurfer segmentation constrained by functional masks; pial/white matter surfaces registered non-linearly (ANTs symmetric normalization); OpenFmriAnalysis toolbox computes layer weights; CSF and white matter layers excluded from analysis; superficial/middle/deep weights used to split β coefficients.
nodes.anchor: Laminar segmentation was performed using co-registered grey and white matter boundaries as references for upper and lower bounds of the segmentation. In order to resolve cortical depth precisely, the curvature of the anatomical boundaries was taken into ac

nodes.text: Voxel selection by first-level t-maps: feature-unspecific (any orientation), feature-specific (left-right contrast), feature-specific BOLD increase (positive t to any orientation); thresholds: top 5%, 10%, 25%
nodes.description: Congruent (Co): voxel preference matches EEG regressor orientation; Incongruent (Inco): opposite; Co-Inco contrast computed; 10% threshold reported in main figures, 5%/25% in supplements.
nodes.anchor: Irrespective of voxel selection, a higher t-value selection threshold indicates higher specificity for the respective stimulus and a lower threshold increases the SNR by including more data.

nodes.text: Cluster permutation test (Maris & Oostenveld 2007) on depth×frequency matrices followed by auto-regressive rank order similarity (aros) test (Clausner & Gentili 2022b) for laminar profiles
nodes.description: Single-tailed cluster test per FOI (alpha 8-14Hz, gamma 50-70Hz) per threshold; significant clusters averaged over frequency at widest point; aros test: rank order of layer averages vs. 25000 permutations of shuffled layer labels; FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) across thresholds.
nodes.anchor: Each significant cluster was then averaged along the frequency dimension at the widest point to enable an auto-regressive rank order similarity (aros) test, testing the laminar activation profile.

nodes.text: Linear mixed-effects models for alpha sub-bands: lower alpha (8-10Hz) vs upper alpha (11-13Hz) defined by median-split around individual peak; Frequency × Congruency (feature-specific) or Frequency × Activation (feature-unspecific) with layer fixed effect, participant random intercepts/slopes
nodes.description: Peak alpha frequency identified in 8-14Hz; median power as reference; ±1Hz around frequencies closest to median below/above peak; β coefficients averaged per sub-band; Wald tests for simple effects; FDR correction across thresholds.
nodes.anchor: After averaging α power over the time window of interest (0.1–0.8 s after stimulus onset), we identified the peak frequency (the frequency showing the largest power decrease within the broad α range 8–14 Hz). We then used the median power across the spectr

nodes.text: What is the layer-specific relationship between alpha/gamma oscillatory activity and feature-specific vs feature-unspecific visual processing in human V1?
nodes.description: Primary research question addressing how cortical oscillations relate to laminar BOLD signals for specific stimulus features versus general activation.
nodes.anchor: The primary aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between cortical oscillations and feature-specific and feature-unspecific BOLD signals across multiple cortical layers.

nodes.text: Does alpha band activity extend beyond widespread inhibition to participate in active feature-specific stimulus processing?
nodes.description: Question motivated by debate on alpha's functional role: global inhibition vs. feature-specific processing.
nodes.anchor: We conclude that the role of α band oscillations extends beyond widespread inhibition and might be involved in active stimulus processing on the level of visual features.

nodes.text: Gamma band activity positively correlates with feature-specific BOLD signals in both superficial and deep cortical layers of V1
nodes.description: Main gamma finding: positive EEG-BOLD relationship for feature-specific processing in superficial and deep layers, not just superficial as previously reported.
nodes.anchor: We could demonstrate that γ band activity positively correlates with feature-specific signals in superficial layers, but we were able to report a deep layer contribution as well.

nodes.text: Alpha band power correlates negatively with both feature-unspecific and feature-specific BOLD signals
nodes.description: Alpha shows negative relationship with BOLD for any stimulus (global modulation) and for feature-specific activity.
nodes.anchor: In addition, we could demonstrate that α band power not only correlates negatively with the feature-unspecific BOLD signal but is related to feature-specific BOLD as well.

nodes.text: Lower frequency alpha (8-10 Hz) predominantly relates to feature-unspecific superficial layer BOLD, while upper frequency alpha (11-13 Hz) relates to feature-specific BOLD in superficial and deep layers
nodes.description: Dissociation of alpha sub-bands by frequency and laminar profile: lower alpha for general modulation in superficial layers, upper alpha for feature-specific processing across layers.
nodes.anchor: Lower frequency α was predominantly related to feature-unspecific superficial layer BOLD, while upper frequency α was found to be related to feature-specific BOLD in superficial and deep layers.

nodes.text: Alpha oscillations serve multiple functionally distinct roles in visual cortex with distinct cortical layer profiles
nodes.description: Conclusion that alpha is not a unitary inhibitory rhythm but comprises sub-bands with different laminar and functional specificities.
nodes.anchor: This study provides the first direct evidence in healthy human participants that low-frequency oscillations serve multiple purposes in the visual cortex, associated with distinct cortical layer profiles.

nodes.text: Individual alpha frequency (IAF) positively correlates with visual task accuracy (d')
nodes.description: Exploratory correlation: higher peak alpha frequency associated with better discrimination performance.
nodes.anchor: We correlated IAF with average response times to correct oddball trials and d′ as a measure for accuracy and found a significant positive correlation between IAF and d′ (p < 0.05).

nodes.text: In 52 participants, gamma-band EEG power (50-70 Hz, 0.1-0.7s post-stimulus) showed positive correlation with feature-specific BOLD increase in superficial and deep layers at 25% voxel threshold (Co-Inco contrast)
nodes.description: Gamma result for feature-specific BOLD increase: significant cluster permutation test at 25% threshold, aros test confirmed laminar profile with strongest effect in superficial and deep layers.
nodes.anchor: For the most liberal threshold (25%) a significant layer profile was obtained, with the strongest relationship between γ and the BOLD signal in superficial and deep cortical layers (see Figure 5—figure supplement 4i).

nodes.text: Alpha-band EEG power (8-14 Hz, 0.2-0.8s post-stimulus) showed negative correlation with feature-unspecific negative BOLD signal, strongest in superficial layers
nodes.description: Feature-unspecific analysis: negative alpha-BOLD relationship for negative BOLD voxels, superficial layer predominance; no significant gamma-BOLD relationship for feature-unspecific activation.
nodes.anchor: While no difference across layers has been observed for the positive BOLD signal, the strongest negative relationship between α and the negative BOLD signal was found in superficial layers.

nodes.text: Feature contrast (Co-Inco) revealed negative alpha-BOLD relationship in superficial and deep layers, driven by upper alpha (11-13 Hz); lower alpha (8-10 Hz) showed no congruency difference
nodes.description: Linear mixed-effects model: significant Frequency × Congruency interaction (pFDR<0.001); simple effects: upper alpha stronger negative for Co vs Inco (pFDR<0.01), lower alpha no difference.
nodes.anchor: This interaction is mainly driven by the upper α sub-band, as indicated by the simple effects analysis. We found a significantly stronger negative relationship of upper α and the BOLD signal for congruent selections (pFDR < 0.01) and the reverse for the in

nodes.text: Feature-specific BOLD increase (Co) showed negative alpha-BOLD relationship (pFDR<0.01) with flat laminar profile except at 25% threshold (superficial > deep)
nodes.description: Alpha effect for strictly positive BOLD voxels: significant for congruent condition only; laminar profile flat at 10% threshold.
nodes.anchor: We observed a negative relationship between the α frequency band and the feature-specific BOLD signal increase for Co (pFDR < 0.01). The laminar profile for Co has been observed to be flat except for the most liberal threshold (25% most activated voxel) wh

nodes.text: Feature-unspecific positive BOLD showed trend-level stronger negative relationship for upper vs lower alpha (pFDR=0.097); negative BOLD showed no sub-band difference
nodes.description: Linear mixed-effects model: significant Frequency × Activation interaction (pFDR<0.05); simple effects: upper alpha more negative for positive BOLD (trend), no difference for negative BOLD.
nodes.anchor: An analysis of simple effects revealed that upper α frequencies are stronger negatively related to the positive BOLD signal as compared to lower α on a trend level (pFDR = 0.097).

nodes.text: Individual alpha frequency (peak 8-14Hz decrease 0.1-0.8s) correlated positively with d' (p<0.05) across 52 participants
nodes.description: Exploratory analysis: IAF from average alpha power spectrum; correlated with d' (accuracy) and RT; significant positive correlation with d'.
nodes.anchor: We exploratively correlated the average IAF during non-oddball trials with the average task accuracy (d′) across participants and indeed found IAF and task performance to be positively correlated.

nodes.text: Temporal SNR was highest in deep layers, not matching the superficial/deep result profiles for alpha/gamma effects
nodes.description: tSNR analysis (two layering algorithms) showed deep layer superiority; result profiles (superficial/deep for gamma, superficial for alpha negative BOLD) do not follow tSNR, arguing against vascular drain artifact.
nodes.anchor: We found that the highest tSNR was obtained from deep layers, as compared to middle and superficial layers. The obtained tSNR is not reflected in any of our result profiles, which strengthens the validity of the here presented results.

nodes.text: Investigate laminar profile of pre-stimulus alpha activity and its relationship to task performance
nodes.description: Pre-stimulus alpha could not be studied due to gradient artifacts until 300ms pre-stimulus; visible pre-stimulus alpha decrease suggests role in task.
nodes.anchor: Due to the limited time window prior to the stimulus onset and gradient artefacts of the MRI machine that lasted until 300 ms before the onset of the stimulus, pre-stimulus α could not be investigated in depth here.

nodes.text: Investigate interactions between lower/upper alpha and gamma oscillations across cortical layers
nodes.description: Phase-amplitude coupling and cross-frequency interactions not examined; future work needed to understand how alpha sub-bands interact with gamma.
nodes.anchor: If and how lower and upper-frequency α band oscillations across different cortical layers interact with each other and how each or both interact with γ band oscillations, needs to be investigated in detail in future experiments.

nodes.text: Test alternative virtual channel selection strategies (feature-specific, cross-frequency) for EEG-fMRI regressors
nodes.description: Current selection maximized SNR using average response; feature-specific or cross-frequency selection could yield different results.
nodes.anchor: Future work might also vary the exact virtual channel selection for obtaining EEG-based regressors. Here, we focused on the grid points with the strongest α or γ response for each frequency band in each hemisphere, derived from the average frequency respon

nodes.text: Incorporate beta band activity in laminar EEG-fMRI studies
nodes.description: Beta hypothesized to play crucial role in visual processing and top-down influence; exploratory analysis found no significant beta-BOLD correlation, possibly due to channel selection optimized for alpha or burst-like beta nature.
nodes.anchor: Furthermore, future experiments might need to consider β band activity as well, as those are hypothesised to play a crucial role for visual stimulus processing and might exert a potential top-down influence.

nodes.text: Conduct experiments manipulating visual features and attention to dissociate upper/lower alpha roles in attended vs suppressed receptive fields
nodes.description: Current study did not manipulate attention; future work needed to test hypothesis that upper alpha reflects feature-specific feedback, lower alpha reflects general attentional modulation.
nodes.anchor: Future experiments manipulating visual features and attention might reveal a differential upper and lower α response to attended visual features and a more general relationship between α (and possibly superficial layer cortical activity) for suppressed (un

nodes.text: Determine directionality and source of gamma deep layer effect using animal model recordings
nodes.description: Correlative human EEG-fMRI cannot resolve directionality; animal recordings needed to test if deep layer gamma reflects feedback, feedforward, or local processing.
nodes.anchor: Conclusive evidence about the directionality and source of the γ-related deep layer effect thus remains uncertain. The correlative nature of the here presented approach cannot provide such insights and are likely better addressed in recordings in animal mo
